newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-OLDTIMERS' LETTERS ARE THE SONGS OF BASEBALL.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-OLDTIMERS' LETTERS ARE THE SONGS OF BASEBALL.

text.p: Songwriter and baseball junkie Seth Swirsky was depressed by the 1994 baseball strike.
So he played some old-time tunes to tease from his memory those lazy days when the crack of a bat and an outfielder loping over green grass after a fly ball was summer's guarantee.

Swirsky, 34 then, really only knew about baseball's halcyon days from devouring statistics, old film clips and the endless yarns that through the years have wrapped themselves lovingly around the game like the red stitching around a baseball.
But he prodded his imagination with the Beatles for a taste of the 1960s, some rock 'n roll from the 50s and big-band swing from the 40s.
Then he began to write letters. Lots of them.
He wrote to some 650 players from the days when baseball really was the national pastime, before greed and outright stupidity strangled what had promised to be one of the best seasons ever.

He wanted to hear directly from the players themselves about the days when they wore baggy, flannel uniforms, thin strips of leather for gloves and spent more time taking batting practice then calls from stockbrokers.
And most of them wanted to tell him about those days that for so many of them obviously defined their lives.
Swirsky received back close to 500 letters and has collected 97 of them in a small book entitled simply, "Baseball Letters."
Browsing through the book, which includes wonderful pictures of the players, is like sifting through the attics of the oldtimers' memories.

It's time-travelling with them to old, downtown stadiums with lattice-work steel girders and wooden seats filled with the pungent aromas of peanuts and beer, the catcalls from fans and the "humma, humma, humma" of chattering infielders.

Swirsky, for instance, wrote to 97-year-old Joe Hauser, who came up to the major leagues in 1922, before a knee injury sent him down to the minors where he hit more than 60 home runs in two different seasons.
"Do you think you could have broken (Babe) Ruth's record of 60 home runs in a season?" asked Swirsky, obviously referring to the major leagues.
Still feisty after all these years, Hauser refused to concede any difference between the major and minor leagues, or even between him and the legendary Sultan of Swat.
"I done broke his record 2 times once in 1930 & the other time in 1933 at Minneapolis, 1930 at Baltimore, surprising you ask a question of that was broken over 50 yrs ago."
Is it true that Ruth, just before he hit a home run in the 1932 World Series, pointed to the centerfield fence and then hit a home run over it?
Woody English, now 89, had no trouble remembering that day and still seemed annoyed by the Ruthian legend about it.
English was playing third base for the Chicago Cubs then and insisted in his letter -- underlining "not" several times -- that Ruth merely held up two fingers indicating there were two outs.
Former Detroit Tiger pitcher Virgil "Fire" Trucks was asked about the first game he pitched in the major leagues.

On his first three pitches, he gave up a single and two doubles. The manager, Trucks relates, came out to the mound and asked catcher Bob Swift: "'Say Bob, doesn't Virgil have it today?' And Bob answered, 'how the hell do I know I haven't caught a pitch yet.'"
Just the attempted explanation of the origins of the name of former pitcher Calvin Coolidge Julius Caesar Tuskahoma McLish is worth the price of the book.
Bobby Thomson's three-run homer in the bottom of the ninth inning to win the 1951 National League pennant for the New York Giants was one of the most dramatic hits ever.

Andy Pafko, the Brooklyn Dodgers' left fielder then, managed to find some consolation in the heartbreaking loss by noting that in most of the pictures showing the homer, "at least I am part of history -- watching the home run ... go over my head."

And Thomson, dubbed "The Flying Scot" for his speed and birthplace in Glasgow, Scotland, wrote: "I have been by myself a few times in my life when the Home run was shown. It's a bit of a thrill by myself more so than when I'm with a group."

Don Larson's response about pitching in 1956 the only perfect game in the World Series wasn't all that unusual. But Swirsky note was: Larsen pitched the greatest game of his life after being served earlier in the day with divorce papers.
Dolph Camilli, who was the National League's Most Valuable Player in 1941, was asked what baseball was like in his day.
"More fun and less money."

Putsy Caballero described the day he broke into the majors at third base for the Philadelphia Phillies in 1944 when he was 16 years old. He ended his note to Swirsky: "Send me a song about baseball when you write one."
Swirsky's book is that song.
